'''''The Simpsons''''' is an American <!-- As per MOS:OPEN, DO NOT add specific genres such as "adult" as those are stated in the infobox and further elaborated in the opening paragraph -->[[animated sitcom]] created by [[Matt Groening]] and developed by Groening, [[James L. Brooks]] and [[Sam Simon]] for the [[Fox Broadcasting Company]]. It is a [[Satire (film and television)|satirical]] depiction of American life, epitomized by the [[Simpson family]], which consists of [[Homer Simpson|Homer]], [[Marge Simpson|Marge]], [[Bart Simpson|Bart]], [[Lisa Simpson|Lisa]], and [[Maggie Simpson|Maggie]]. Set in the fictional town of [[Springfield (The Simpsons)|Springfield]], in an unspecified location in the United States, it caricatures society, [[Western culture]], television, and the [[human condition]].

The family was conceived by Groening shortly before a solicitation for a series of [[The Simpsons shorts|animated shorts]] with producer Brooks. He created a [[dysfunctional family]] and named the characters after his own family members, substituting Bart for his own name; he thought Simpson was a funny name in that it sounded similar to "[[simpleton]]".<ref name="smithsonian">{{cite magazine |last=De La Roca |first=Claudia |date=May 2012 |title=Matt Groening Reveals the Location of the Real Springfield |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/matt-groening-reveals-the-location-of-the-real-springfield-60583379/ |magazine=[[Smithsonian (magazine)|Smithsonian]] |access-date=December 6, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210910151244/https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/matt-groening-reveals-the-location-of-the-real-springfield-60583379/ |archive-date=September 10, 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> The shorts became a part of ''[[The Tracey Ullman Show]]'' on April 19, 1987. After three seasons, the sketch was developed into a half-hour primetime show and became Fox's first series to land in the Top 30 ratings in a season (1989–1990).

Since its debut on December 17, 1989, [[List of The Simpsons episodes|{{Template parameter value|The Simpsons|Infobox television||num_episodes}} episodes]] of the show have been broadcast. It is the [[List of longest-running American television series|longest-running American animated series]], [[List of longest-running American primetime television series|longest-running American sitcom]], and the [[List of longest-running scripted American primetime television series|longest-running American scripted primetime television series]], both in seasons and individual episodes. A feature-length film, ''[[The Simpsons Movie]]'' (2007), was released in theaters worldwide to critical and commercial success, with [[The New Simpsons Movie|a sequel]] set to release in 2027. The series has also spawned numerous [[List of The Simpsons comics|comic book series]], [[List of The Simpsons video games|video games]], [[List of The Simpsons books|books]] and other related media, as well as a billion-dollar [[The Simpsons (franchise)#Merchandise|merchandising industry]]. ''The Simpsons'' was initially a joint production by [[Gracie Films]] and [[20th Television]].<ref>{{cite web |title=About The Simpsons |url=https://www.fox.com/the-simpsons/article/about-the-show-597bbd8a7600a0002278f4c6/ |website=[[Fox Broadcasting Company|Fox]] |access-date=April 24, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190425041925/https://www.fox.com/the-simpsons/article/about-the-show-597bbd8a7600a0002278f4c6/ |archive-date=April 25, 2019 |url-status=dead}}</ref> In March 2021, 20th Television launched [[20th Television Animation]], a new production unit overseeing ''The Simpsons'' and its other animated series.<ref>{{cite web |last=Nakamura |first=Reid |date=March 30, 2021 |title=20th Television Launches Animation Unit Led by Marci Proietto |url=https://www.thewrap.com/20th-television-launches-animation-unit-led-by-marci-proietto/ |website=[[TheWrap]] |access-date=September 16, 2026}}</ref> On April 2, 2025, the show was renewed for four additional seasons on Fox, with 15 episodes and up to four [[Disney+]] specials each.

''The Simpsons'' received widespread critical acclaim throughout its early seasons in the 1990s, which are generally considered its "golden age". Since then, it has been criticized for a perceived decline in quality. ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' named it the 20th century's best television series<ref name="TimeBestCentury">{{cite magazine |date=December 31, 1999 |title=The Best of the Century |url=https://time.com/archive/6737430/the-best-of-the-century/ |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |access-date=September 15, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150330092341/http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,993039,00.html |archive-date=March 30, 2015 |url-status=live}}</ref> while Erik Adams of ''[[The A.V. Club]]'' named it "television's crowning achievement regardless of format".<ref>{{cite web |last=Adams |first=Erik |date=February 16, 2015 |title=The Best Animated Series Ever, from Adventure Time to Whatever the Zeta Project Is |url=https://www.avclub.com/the-best-animated-series-ever-from-adventure-time-to-w-1798277370 |website=[[The A.V. Club]] |at=§ "S: The Simpsons" |access-date=January 15, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150906115412/http://www.avclub.com/article/best-animated-series-ever-adventure-time-whatever--214799 |archive-date=September 6, 2015 |url-status=live}}</ref> The Simpson family was awarded a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] on January 14, 2000. It has [[List of awards and nominations received by The Simpsons|won dozens of awards]] since it debuted as a series, including 37 [[Primetime Emmy Award]]s, 34 [[Annie Award]]s, and 2 [[Peabody Award]]s. Homer's exclamatory catchphrase of "[[D'oh!]]" has been adopted into the [[English language]]. Upon its debut, ''The Simpsons'' was often credited with changing comedy on television<ref>{{cite web |last=Dowling |first=Stephen |date=December 17, 2014 |title=How The Simpsons Changed TV |url=https://www.bbc.com/culture/article/20141216-how-the-simpsons-changed-tv |website=BBC Culture |access-date=February 3, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260203070923/https://www.bbc.com/culture/article/20141216-how-the-simpsons-changed-tv |archive-date=February 3, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> and is noted for inspiring many other later adult-oriented, popular animated sitcom television series.<!--The impending Futurama/Family Guy crossovers are mentioned in the 'Influence on TV' section. They do not need to be mentioned here.-->

==Premise==

===Characters===
{{Main|List of The Simpsons characters|l1 = List of ''The Simpsons'' characters}}

The main characters are the [[Simpson family]], who live in the fictional "[[Middle America (United States)|Middle America]]" town of Springfield.{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=28}} [[Homer Simpson|Homer]], the father, works as a safety inspector at the [[Springfield Nuclear Power Plant]], a position at odds with his careless, buffoonish personality. He is married to [[Marge Simpson|Marge]] ({{nee}} Bouvier), a stereotypical American housewife and mother. They have three children: [[Bart Simpson|Bart]], a ten-year-old troublemaker and prankster; [[Lisa Simpson|Lisa]], a precocious eight-year-old activist; and [[Maggie Simpson|Maggie]], the baby of the family who rarely speaks, but communicates by sucking on a pacifier. Although the family is dysfunctional, many episodes examine their relationships and bonds with each other, and they are often shown to care about one another.<ref>{{cite AV media |people=[[Matt Groening]], [[Bill Oakley]], [[Josh Weinstein]], [[Jon Vitti]], and [[Susie Dietter]] (commentators) |date=December 13, 2005 |chapter=Commentary for "Home Sweet Homediddly-Dum-Doodily" |title=The Simpsons: The Complete Seventh Season |type=DVD audio commentary |publisher=[[20th Century Fox Home Entertainment]]}}</ref>

===Continuity and the floating timeline===
Despite the depiction of yearly milestones such as holidays or birthdays passing, the characters never age. The series uses a [[floating timeline]] in which episodes generally take place in the year the episode is produced. Flashbacks and flashforwards do occasionally depict the characters at other points in their lives, with the timeline of these depictions also generally floating relative to the year the episode is produced. Regarding the contradictory flashbacks, Selman stated that "they all kind of happened in their imaginary world".<ref>{{cite web |last=Bailey |first=Kat |date=July 28, 2021 |title=The Simpsons: Matt Selman On Continuity And His Support For a Simpsons Hit & Run Remake |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/matt-selman-simpsons-hit-and-run-remake |access-date=July 28, 2021 |website=[[IGN]] |archive-date=September 2, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210902020309/https://www.ign.com/articles/matt-selman-simpsons-hit-and-run-remake?fbclid=IwAR2dNT3h2bwJAkw8gY72mmgn3f1ndf20KP7iWER4cETTmlkoSbMX7TORVns/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Setting===
{{Main|Springfield (The Simpsons)|l1 = Springfield {{(-}}''The Simpsons'')}}

''The Simpsons'' takes place in a fictional American town called [[Springfield (The Simpsons)|Springfield]]. The show is intentionally evasive with regard to Springfield's location.{{sfn|Turner|2004|pp=289–290}} Springfield's geography and that of its surroundings are inconsistent: from one episode to another, it may have coastlines, deserts, vast farmland, mountains, or whatever the story or joke requires.{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=30}} Groening has said that Springfield has much in common with [[Portland, Oregon]], the city where he grew up.<ref>{{cite news |last=Hamilton |first=Don |date=July 19, 2002 |title=Matt Groening's Portland |url=http://www.portlandtribune.com/news/story.php?story_id=12392 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070224031814/http://www.portlandtribune.com/news/story.php?story_id=12392 |archive-date=February 24, 2007 |url-status=dead |work=[[Portland Tribune]]}}</ref> Groening has said that he named it after [[Springfield, Oregon]], and the fictitious Springfield which was the setting of the series ''[[Father Knows Best]]''. He "figured out that Springfield was one of the most common names for a city in the U.S. In anticipation of the success of the show, I thought, 'This will be cool; everyone will think it's their Springfield.' And they do."<ref name="smithsonian" />

When producer [[James L. Brooks]] was working on the television variety show ''[[The Tracey Ullman Show]]'', he decided to include small animated sketches before and after the commercial breaks. Having seen one of cartoonist [[Matt Groening]]'s ''[[Life in Hell]]'' comic strips, Brooks asked Groening to pitch an idea for a series of animated shorts. Groening initially intended to present an animated version of his ''Life in Hell'' series.<ref name="americasfirstfamily">{{cite AV media |people=Ralph Lee (director); Elaine Shepherd (producer) |date=June 23, 2000 |title=The Simpsons: America's First Family |type=Television documentary |publisher=[[BBC Two]]}}</ref> However, Groening later realized that animating ''Life in Hell'' would require the rescinding of [[publication right]]s for his life's work. He therefore chose another approach while waiting in the lobby of Brooks's office for the pitch meeting, hurriedly formulating his version of a dysfunctional family that became the Simpsons.<ref name="americasfirstfamily" /><ref>{{cite interview |last=Groening |first=Matt |subject-link=Matt Groening |interviewer=[[David Bianculli]] |date=February 14, 2003 |title=Simpson's Creator Matt Groening |url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=1162008 |work=[[Fresh Air]] |publisher=[[NPR]] |access-date=August 8, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071213045217/http://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=1162008 |archive-date=December 13, 2007 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The Simpson family first appeared as [[The Simpsons shorts|shorts]] in ''The Tracey Ullman Show'' on April 19, 1987.{{sfn|Richmond & Coffman|1997|p=14}} Groening submitted only basic sketches to the animators and assumed that the figures would be cleaned up in production. The suit said she should receive a share of the profits of ''The Simpsons''<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Spotnitz |first=Frank |date=October 23, 1992 |title=Eat My Shorts! |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |page=8 |url=https://ew.com/article/1992/10/23/tracey-ullman-sues-fox/ |access-date=January 15, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111016142946/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,312110,00.html |archive-date=October 16, 2011 |url-status=live }}</ref>—a claim rejected by the courts.<ref>{{cite news |date=October 21, 1992 |title=Ullman loses 'Simpsons' suit |url=https://variety.com/1992/biz/news/ullman-loses-simpsons-suit-101001/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131012110513/http://variety.com/1992/biz/news/ullman-loses-simpsons-suit-101001/ |archive-date=October 12, 2013 |access-date=August 24, 2011 |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |agency=Associated Press}}</ref>

===Animation===
[[File:David Silverman in 2007-cropped.JPG|right|thumb|upright|Animation director [[David Silverman (animator)|David Silverman]], who helped define the look of the show<ref name="silverman" />]]
Several different American and international studios animate ''The Simpsons''. Throughout the run of the animated shorts on ''The Tracey Ullman Show'', the animation was produced domestically at [[Klasky Csupo]].<ref name="animation" /> With the debut of the series, because of an increased workload, Fox subcontracted production to several local and foreign studios.<ref name="animation" />

For the first three seasons, Klasky Csupo animated ''The Simpsons'' in the United States. In 1992, the show's production company, Gracie Films, switched domestic production to [[Film Roman]],<ref>{{cite news |last=Bernstein |first=Sharon |date=January 21, 1992 |title='The Simpsons' Producer Changes Animation Firms |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1992-01-21-fi-739-story.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120618113432/http://articles.latimes.com/1992-01-21/business/fi-739_1_bart-simpson |archive-date=June 18, 2012 |access-date=January 15, 2022 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |page=18}}</ref> which handled the work until the season 28 production cycle, when it moved to [[Fox Television Animation]].<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Fletcher |first=Kevin Alan |date=2025 |title=The Family Dynamic as Enduring Form in United States Media Culture |type=PhD thesis |publisher=University of Otago |page=145 |url=https://hdl.handle.net/10523/44604 |access-date=September 16, 2026}}</ref> In the first episode of [[The Simpsons season 14|Season 14]], production switched from traditional [[cel animation]] to [[digital ink and paint]].<ref>{{cite AV media |people=[[Matt Groening]], [[Al Jean]], [[Jeffrey Lynch]], [[Mike Reiss]], and [[David Silverman (animator)|David Silverman]] (commentators) |date=June 15, 2004 |chapter=Commentary for "Whacking Day" |title=The Simpsons: The Complete Fourth Season |type=DVD audio commentary |publisher=[[20th Century Fox Home Entertainment]]}}</ref> The first episode to experiment with digital coloring was "[[Radioactive Man (The Simpsons episode)|Radioactive Man]]" in 1995. Animators used digital ink and paint during production of the [[The Simpsons season 12|season 12]] episode "[[Tennis the Menace]]", but Gracie Films delayed the regular use of digital ink and paint until two seasons later. The already completed "Tennis the Menace" was broadcast as made.<ref name="Grala2007">{{cite magazine |last=Grala |first=Alyson |date=May 2007 |title=A Salute to The Simpsons |url=http://www.license-europe.com/licensemag/data/articlestandard//licensemag/192007/425752/article.pdf |magazine=License! |page=14 |format=PDF |access-date=August 11, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070925213323/http://www.license-europe.com/licensemag/data/articlestandard//licensemag/192007/425752/article.pdf |archive-date=September 25, 2007 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
The production staff at the American animation studio, Film Roman, drew [[storyboard]]s, designed new characters, backgrounds, props and drew character and background layouts, which became [[animatic]]s screened for the writers at Gracie Films for any changes to be made before the work was shipped overseas. The overseas studios then drew the [[Inbetweening|inbetweens]], inked and painted, and rendered the animation to tape before it was shipped back to the United States to be delivered to Fox three to four months later.<ref>{{cite news |last=Elber |first=Lynn |date=August 5, 2001 |title=TV's 'The Simpsons' Goes Global |agency=Associated Press}}</ref>

The series began [[high-definition television|high-definition]] production in season 20; the first episode, "[[Take My Life, Please]]", aired February 15, 2009. The move to HDTV included a new opening sequence.<ref>{{cite press release |date=January 23, 2009 |title=Primetime Listings (February 8–14) |url=http://www.foxflash.com/div.php/main/page?aID=1z4&mo=2&d=10 |publisher=[[Fox Broadcasting Company|Fox]] |access-date=January 24, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090201143538/http://www.foxflash.com/div.php/main/page?aID=1z4&mo=2&d=10 |archive-date=February 1, 2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Matt Groening called it a complicated change because it affected the timing and composition of animation.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ryan |first=Kyle |date=March 25, 2009 |title=Matt Groening |url=https://www.avclub.com/matt-groening-1798216089 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111113031416/http://www.avclub.com/articles/matt-groening,25525/1/ |archive-date=November 13, 2011 |access-date=January 15, 2022 |website=[[The A.V. ==Themes==
{{Main|Media in The Simpsons|Politics in The Simpsons|Religion in The Simpsons|l1 = Media in ''The Simpsons''|l2 = Politics in ''The Simpsons''|l3 = Religion in ''The Simpsons''}}

''The Simpsons'' uses the standard setup of a situational comedy, or sitcom, as its premise. The series centers on a family and their life in a typical American town,{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=28}} serving as a [[satirical]] parody of a [[American middle class|middle-class]] [[American lifestyle]].<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Flew |first=Terry |date=May 2, 1994 |title=The Simpsons: Culture, Class and Popular TV |url=http://www.metromagazine.com.au/magazine/backisues.asp?keywords=cultu&whichpage=12&pagesize=15 |magazine=Metro |issue=97 |pages=14–19 |access-date=June 13, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110722074356/http://www.metromagazine.com.au/magazine/backisues.asp?keywords=cultu&whichpage=12&pagesize=15 |archive-date=July 22, 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref> However, because of its animated nature, ''The Simpsons''{{'}} scope is larger than that of a regular sitcom. The town of Springfield acts as a complete universe in which characters can explore the issues faced by modern society. By having Homer work in a [[nuclear power plant]], the show can comment on the state of the environment.{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=55}} Through Bart and Lisa's days at [[Springfield Elementary School]], the show's writers illustrate pressing or controversial issues in the field of education. The town features a vast array of television channels, which enables the producers to make jokes about the entertainment industry and the press.{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=388}}

[[Al Jean]] acknowledged in an interview that "We [the show] are of [[Modern liberalism in the United States|liberal]] bent."{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=223}} The writers often evince an appreciation for [[Progressivism|progressive leanings]], but the show makes jokes across the political spectrum.{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=224}} The show portrays government and large corporations as evil entities that take advantage of the common worker.{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=223}} In ''The Simpsons'', politicians are corrupt, ministers such as [[Reverend Lovejoy]] are dismissive to churchgoers, and the local police force is incompetent.{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=56}} Religion also figures as a recurring theme.<ref>{{cite book |last=Myles |first=Robert J. |date=February 26, 2015 |chapter=Biblical Literacy and The Simpsons |title=Rethinking Biblical Literacy |editor-last=Edwards |editor-first=Katie B. |location=London |publisher=Bloomsbury T&T Clark |pages=143–162 |doi=10.5040/9780567662040.ch-007 |isbn=978-0-56740-321-6}}</ref> In times of crisis, the family often turns to God, and the show has dealt with most of the major religions.<ref>{{cite news |last=Pinsky |first=Mark I |date=August 15, 1999 |title=The Gospel According to Homer |work=[[Orlando Sentinel]]}}</ref>

==Hallmarks==

===Opening sequence===
{{Main|The Simpsons opening sequence|l1 = ''The Simpsons'' opening sequence}}

The standard opening has gone through three iterations (a replacement of some shots at the start of the second season, and a brand-new sequence when the show switched to high-definition in 2009).<ref>{{cite news |last=Leonard |first=Tom |date=February 17, 2009 |title='The Simpsons' opening sequence changes |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/tvandradio/4682314/The-Simpsons-opening-sequence-changes.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090220191329/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/tvandradio/4682314/The-Simpsons-opening-sequence-changes.html |archive-date=February 20, 2009 |access-date=March 2, 2009 |work=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |location=London}}</ref>

Each has the same basic sequence of events: the camera zooms through [[cumulus cloud]]s, through the show's title towards the town of [[Springfield (The Simpsons)|Springfield]]. The camera then follows the members of the family on their way home. Upon entering their house, the Simpsons settle down on their couch to watch television. The original opening was created by [[David Silverman (animator)|David Silverman]], and was the first task he did when production began on the show.<ref name="silverinter">{{cite web |title=Top titles |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/cult/simpsons/interviews/silverman/page4.shtml |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111119123229/http://www.bbc.co.uk/cult/simpsons/interviews/silverman/page4.shtml |archive-date=November 19, 2011 |access-date=August 1, 2007 |website=BBC}}</ref> The series' distinctive [[The Simpsons Theme|theme song]] was [[composer|composed]] by musician [[Danny Elfman]] in 1989.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Simpsons |url=https://www.dannyelfman.com/television/the-simpsons |website=Danny Elfman |access-date=September 15, 2026}}</ref>

One of the most distinctive aspects of the opening is that three of its elements change from episode to episode: Bart writes different things on the school chalkboard,<ref name="silverinter" /> Lisa plays different solos on her saxophone (or occasionally a different instrument), and different gags accompany the family as they enter their living room to sit on the couch (colloquially dubbed "couch gags").{{sfn|Richmond & Coffman|1997|pp=90–91}}

===Halloween episodes===
{{Main|Treehouse of Horror|l1 = ''Treehouse of Horror''}}

[[File:Bart Night Gallery.jpg|thumb|Bart Simpson introducing a segment of "[[Treehouse of Horror IV]]" in the manner of [[Rod Serling]]'s ''[[Night Gallery]]'']]
The special [[Halloween]] episode has become an annual tradition. "[[Treehouse of Horror (The Simpsons episode)|Treehouse of Horror]]" was first broadcast in 1990 as part of [[The Simpsons season 2|season two]] and established the pattern of three separate, self-contained stories in each Halloween episode.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Martyn |first1=Warren |last2=Wood |first2=Adrian |year=2000 |title=The Simpsons Halloween Special |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/cult/simpsons/episodeguide/season2/page3.shtml |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101103060830/http://www.bbc.co.uk/cult/simpsons/episodeguide/season2/page3.shtml |archive-date=November 3, 2010 |access-date=November 9, 2007 |website=BBC}}</ref> These pieces usually involve the family in some horror, science fiction, or supernatural setting and often parody or pay homage to a famous piece of work in those genres.{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=31}} They always take place outside the normal continuity of the show.

===Humor===
The show's humor turns on cultural references that cover a wide spectrum of society so that viewers from all generations can enjoy the show. The animators also regularly add jokes or sight gags into the show's background via humorous or incongruous bits of text in signs, newspapers, [[billboards]], and elsewhere. Kristin Thompson argues that ''The Simpsons'' uses a "flurry of cultural references, intentionally inconsistent characterization, and considerable self-reflexivity about television conventions and the status of the programme as a television show."{{sfn|Thompson|2003|p=139}}

One of Bart's early [[wiktionary:hallmark#English|hallmarks]] was his prank calls to [[Moe's Tavern]] owner [[Moe Szyslak]] where he asks for a [[gag name]]. Moe tries to find that person in the bar, but soon realizes it is a prank call and angrily threatens Bart. These calls were apparently based on a series of prank calls known as the [[Tube Bar prank calls|Tube Bar recordings]], though Groening has denied any causal connection.<ref>{{cite news |last=Ehrman |first=Mark |date=June 3, 1993 |title=Telephone Trespassing |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1993-06-03-vw-42985-story.html |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |access-date=January 15, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203211508/http://articles.latimes.com/1993-06-03/news/vw-42985_1_prank-calls |archive-date=December 3, 2013 |url-status=live}}</ref>
''The Simpsons'' also often includes [[self-referential humor]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Strachan |first=Al |date=March 10, 2009 |title=Doh! The Simpson's sets a record by staying relevant |work=[[The Vancouver Sun]]}}</ref> The most common form is jokes about Fox Broadcasting.<ref>{{cite news |last=Burkeman |first=Oliver |date=June 30, 2007 |title=Embiggening the smallest man |url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2007/jun/30/film.filmnews |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131013021744/http://www.theguardian.com/media/2007/jun/30/film.filmnews |archive-date=October 13, 2013 |access-date=August 24, 2009 |work=[[The Guardian]] |location=London}}</ref>

The show uses [[catchphrase]]s, and most of the primary and secondary characters have at least one each.{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=60}} Notable expressions include Homer's annoyed grunt "[[D'oh!]]", Mr. Burns' "Excellent" and [[Nelson Muntz]]'s "''Ha''-ha!" The episode "[[Bart Gets Famous]]" mocks catchphrase-based humor, as Bart achieves fame on the ''Krusty the Clown Show'' solely for saying "I didn't do it".{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=61}}

====Purported foreshadowing of actual events====
{{main|The Simpsons future predictions|l1 = ''The Simpsons'' future predictions}}

''The Simpsons'' has gained notoriety for jokes that appeared to become reality. Perhaps the most famous example comes from the episode "[[Bart to the Future]]", which mentions billionaire [[Donald Trump]] having been president of the United States at one time and leaving the nation broke. The episode first aired in 2000, sixteen years before Trump (who at the time was [[Donald Trump 2000 presidential campaign|exploring a presidential run]]) was elected.<ref>{{cite news |last=Clark |first=Charles |date=November 9, 2016 |title=The Simpsons predicted a Donald Trump presidency 16 years ago |url=http://www.businessinsider.com/the-simpsons-predicted-a-donald-trump-presidency-2016-11?r=UK&IR=T |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180101135402/http://www.businessinsider.com/the-simpsons-predicted-a-donald-trump-presidency-2016-11?r=UK&IR=T |archive-date=January 1, 2018 |access-date=December 31, 2017 |work=[[Business Insider]]}}</ref>

[[Al Jean]] has commented on the show's purported ability to predict the future, explaining that they are really just "educated guesses" and stating that "if you throw enough darts, you're going to get some bullseyes."<ref name="nme">{{cite web |last=McMahon |first=James |date=November 16, 2021 |title='The Simpsons' showrunner on uncanny predictions: "9/11 was bizarre" |url=https://www.nme.com/news/tv/the-simpsons-al-jean-predictions-911-3096871 |access-date=January 10, 2024 |website=[[NME]] |archive-date=November 19, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211119152732/https://www.nme.com/news/tv/the-simpsons-al-jean-predictions-911-3096871 |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Fact-checking]] sources such as [[Snopes]] have debunked many of the claimed prophecies, explaining that the show's extensive run means "a lot of jokes, and a lot of opportunities for coincidences to appear" and "most of these 'predictions' have rather simple and mundane explanations".<ref>{{cite web |date=February 6, 2017 |title='The Simpsons' Didn't Predict That |url=https://www.snopes.com/collections/the-simpsons-didnt-predict-that/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211019185618/https://www.snopes.com/collections/the-simpsons-didnt-predict-that/ |archive-date=October 19, 2021 |access-date=December 26, 2019 |website=[[Snopes]]}}</ref>

===Television===
''The Simpsons'' was the first successful animated program in American prime-time since ''[[Wait Till Your Father Gets Home]]'' in the 1970s.{{sfn|Alberti|2003|p=xii}} During most of the 1980s, American pundits considered animated shows as appropriate only for children, and animating a show was too expensive to achieve a quality suitable for prime-time television. ''The Simpsons'' changed this perception,<ref name="animation" /> initially leading to a short period where networks attempted to recreate prime-time cartoon success with shows like ''[[Capitol Critters]]'', ''[[Fish Police (TV series)|Fish Police]]'', and ''[[Family Dog (TV series)|Family Dog]]'', which were expensive and unsuccessful.<ref>{{cite news |last=Cerone |first=Daniel |date=February 28, 1992 |title='Fish Police' on Endangered Species List |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1992-02-28-ca-2993-story.html |access-date=January 15, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305020006/http://articles.latimes.com/1992-02-28/entertainment/ca-2993_1_prime-time-programs |archive-date=March 5, 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref> ''The Simpsons''{{'}} use of Korean animation studios for [[tweening]], coloring, and filming made the episodes cheaper. The success of ''The Simpsons'' and the lower production cost prompted American television networks to take chances on other adult animated series.<ref name="animation" /> This development led American producers to a 1990s boom in new, animated prime-time shows for adults, such as ''[[Beavis and Butt-Head]]'', ''[[South Park]]'', ''[[Family Guy]]'', ''[[King of the Hill]]'', ''[[Futurama]]'' (which was created by Matt Groening), and ''[[The Critic (TV series)|The Critic]]'' (which was also produced by Gracie Films).<ref name="animation" /> For ''Family Guy'' creator [[Seth MacFarlane]], "''The Simpsons'' created an audience for prime-time animation that had not been there for many, many years ... === Australian broadcast ===
In Australia, ''The Simpsons'' debuted on February 10, 1991 on [[Ten Network]], becoming series' first international broadcast.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/129094164?searchTerm=%22The%20Simpsons%22 |title=The family that all fuss about |date=September 4, 1991 |work=[[The Canberra Times]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://ufdc.ufl.edu/AA00090087/01337/images/4 |title=The Simpsons make Australian debut |date=September 11, 1991 |work=[[Sanford Herald]]}}</ref> It aired on Ten Network up until 2017.<ref>{{cite news |last=Donoughue |first=Paul |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2017-10-13/the-simpsons-off-free-to-air-after-fox-pulls-content-network-ten/9042134 |title=The Simpsons disappears from Australian free-to-air TV after Fox pulls content from Ten Network |date=October 12, 2017 |work=[[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]]}}</ref> After leaving the Ten Network the show moved to [[7mate]] on February 23, 2018 with the premiere of its 28th season.<ref>{{cite web |last=Knox |first=David |date=February 13, 2018 |title=Returning: The Simpsons |url=https://tvtonight.com.au/2018/02/returning-the-simpsons-8.html |website=TV Tonight |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210927164247/https://tvtonight.com.au/2018/02/returning-the-simpsons-8.html |archive-date=September 27, 2021 |access-date=November 9, 2026}}</ref> The show then moved to [[Disney+]] where it has stayed since its [[The Simpsons season 33|33rd season]].

===Canadian broadcast===
In Canada, ''The Simpsons'' has aired on several national networks throughout the years. Historically [[CBC Television|CBC]] once held Canadian syndication rights for the series until 2006, airing episodes on weekdays at 5pm. On [[Global Television Network|Global]] and its affiliates, ''The Simpsons'' aired on simulcast from [[The Simpsons season 1|season 1]] up until [[The Simpsons season 29|season 29]]. [[The Simpsons season 30|Season 30]] saw the series move to [[Citytv]] until [[The Simpsons season 32|season 32]]. The series moved to [[CHCH-DT]] for seasons [[The Simpsons season 33|33]] and [[The Simpsons season 34|34]] before beginning to share Canadian broadcasting rights with Citytv starting with [[The Simpsons season 35|season 35]]. Despite the rare schedule changes, ''The Simpsons'' has generally kept to the same timeslot as [[Fox Broadcasting Company|FOX]].

===Renewals===
On April 2, 2025, Fox renewed ''The Simpsons'' for four additional seasons (seasons 37 through 40) through the 2028–2029 television season, coinciding with the show's 40th anniversary. Each season consists of 15 episodes.<ref>{{cite news |last=Andreeva |first=Nellie |date=April 2, 2025 |title=Fox Picks Up Four Seasons of 'The Simpsons', 'Family Guy', 'Bob's Burgers' & Returning 'American Dad!' in Mega Deal with Disney TV Studios |url=https://deadline.com/2025/04/the-simpsons-family-guy-bobs-burgers-american-dad-renewed-1236356360/ |access-date=April 4, 2025 |work=[[Deadline Hollywood]]}}</ref>

===Syndication===
In the United States, the cable television network [[FXX]] obtained [[broadcast syndication|exclusive cable and digital syndication]] rights for ''The Simpsons''. Original contracts had previously stated that syndication rights for ''The Simpsons'' would not be sold to cable until the series conclusion, at a time when cable syndication deals were highly rare. The series has been syndicated to local broadcast stations in nearly all markets throughout the United States since September 1994.<ref>{{cite news |last=Andreeva |first=Nellie |date=November 15, 2013 |title=FXX Lands 'The Simpsons' in Biggest Off-Network Deal in TV History |url=https://deadline.com/2013/11/fxx-lands-the-simpsons-in-the-biggest-off-network-deal-in-tv-history-635800/ |access-date=September 15, 2026 |work=[[Deadline Hollywood]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241202205047/https://deadline.com/2013/11/fxx-lands-the-simpsons-in-the-biggest-off-network-deal-in-tv-history-635800/ |archive-date=December 2, 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

==={{visible anchor|Criticism|Criticism and controversy}}===

====Controversy====
Bart's rebellious, bad boy nature, which underlies his misbehavior and rarely leads to any punishment, led some people to characterize him as a poor [[role model]] for children.{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=131}}<ref>{{cite news |last=Rosenbaum |first=Martin |date=June 29, 2007 |title=Is ''The Simpsons'' Still Subversive? |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/6252856.stm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070708072703/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/6252856.stm |archive-date=July 8, 2007 |access-date=August 6, 2007 |work=[[BBC News]]}}</ref> In schools, educators claimed that Bart was a "threat to learning" because of his "underachiever and proud of it" attitude and negative attitude regarding his education.<ref>{{cite news |last=Freedman |first=Donna |date=June 2, 1990 |title=Is Bart a Brat? Popular Cartoon Kid as Annoying to Some as He Is Funny to Others |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]]}}</ref> Others described him as "egotistical, aggressive and mean-spirited".<ref>{{cite news |last=Dunne |first=Mike |date=June 1, 1990 |title=Bart Simpson: Cool Dude or Smart-Aleck Menace? |work=[[The Sacramento Bee]]}}</ref> In a 1991 interview, [[Bill Cosby]] described Bart as a bad role model for children, calling him "angry, confused, frustrated". In response, Matt Groening said, "That sums up Bart, all right. Most people are in a struggle to be normal [and] <!--Note, this is an exact copy of the quote (except for the added "[and]"). The original article did not use any punctuation here-->he thinks normal is very boring, and does things that others just wished they dare do."<ref>{{cite news |date=September 25, 1991 |title=A Badder Bart |work=[[The Record (Bergen County)|The Record]]}}</ref> On January 27, 1992, then-President [[George H. W. Bush]] said, "We are going to keep on trying to strengthen the American family, to make American families a lot more like [[the Waltons]] and a lot less like the Simpsons."<ref name="mikescully">{{cite magazine |last=Griffiths |first=Nick |date=April 15, 2000 |title=America's First Family |url=http://snpp.com/other/articles/firstfamily.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140811014602/http://www.snpp.com/other/articles/firstfamily.html |archive-date=August 11, 2014 |magazine=The Times Magazine |pages=25, 27–28 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The writers rushed out a tongue-in-cheek reply in the form of a short segment that aired three days later before a rerun of "[[Stark Raving Dad]]" in which Bart replied, "Hey, we're just like the Waltons. We're praying for an end to [[the Depression]], too."{{sfn|Turner|2004|pp=230–231}}<ref name="OrtvedVanityFair" />

The show also received criticism from the nuclear power industry in its early years, with its portrayal of the evil boss Mr. Burns and "bungling idiot" employees (including Homer Simpson himself) with their lack of safety and security.<ref name="nuclear">{{cite news |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=December 6, 1990 |title=Nuclear industry having meltdown over Simpsons |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=7cYfAAAAIBAJ&sjid=uNgEAAAAIBAJ&pg=1118%2C5123046 |access-date=July 18, 2022 |work=[[Southeast Missourian]] |archive-date=April 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230405232227/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=7cYfAAAAIBAJ&sjid=uNgEAAAAIBAJ&pg=1118,5123046 |url-status=live}}</ref> In a letter to the nuclear power-backed [[Nuclear Energy Institute|U.S. Council for Energy Awareness]], producer Sam Simon apologized, stating, "I apologize that the Simpsons have offended a lot of people in the energy industry. I agree with you that in real life, Homer Simpson would not be employed at a nuclear power plant. On the other hand, he probably wouldn't be employed anywhere."<ref name="nuclear" />

Various episodes of the show have generated controversy. The Simpsons visit Australia in "[[Bart vs. Australia]]" ([[The Simpsons season 6|season six]], 1995) and Brazil in "[[Blame It on Lisa]]" ([[The Simpsons season 13|season 13]], 2002), and both episodes generated controversy and negative reaction in the visited countries.<ref>{{cite news |last=Carroll |first=Steven |date=March 17, 2009 |title=Cartoon Family Gets Animated on First Irish Visit |url=https://www.irishtimes.com/newspaper/ireland/2009/0317/1224242946443.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121017062621/http://www.irishtimes.com/newspaper/ireland/2009/0317/1224242946443.html |archive-date=October 17, 2012 |access-date=April 15, 2009 |newspaper=[[The Irish Times]] |url-status=dead}}</ref> In the latter case, Rio de Janeiro's tourist board—which claimed that the city was portrayed as having rampant street crime, kidnappings, slums, and monkey and rat infestations—went so far as to threaten Fox with legal action.<ref>{{cite news |date=April 15, 2002 |title=Simpsons Apologize to Rio |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/1931551.stm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120325070037/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/1931551.stm |archive-date=March 25, 2012 |access-date=March 17, 2009 |work=[[BBC News]]}}</ref> Groening was a fierce and vocal critic of the episode "[[A Star Is Burns]]" (season 6, 1995), which featured a [[fictional crossover|crossover]] with ''[[The Critic (TV series)|The Critic]]''. He felt that it was just an advertisement for ''The Critic'', and that people would incorrectly associate the show with him. When he was unsuccessful in getting the episode pulled, he had his name removed from the credits and went public with his concerns, openly criticizing James L. Brooks and saying the episode "violates the Simpsons' universe". In response, Brooks said, "I am furious with Matt, ... he's allowed his opinion, but airing this publicly in the press is going too far. ... his behavior right now is rotten."<ref name="LATimes">{{cite news |last=Brennan |first=Judy |date=March 3, 1995 |title=Matt Groening's Reaction to The Critic's First Appearance on The Simpsons |work=[[Los Angeles Times]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Richmond |first=Ray |date=March 4, 1995 |title=Groening's Point Well-Taken, but Probably Best Made Privately |work=[[Los Angeles Daily News]]}}</ref>

"[[The Principal and the Pauper]]" ([[The Simpsons season 9|season nine]], 1997) is one of the most controversial episodes of ''The Simpsons''. Many fans and critics reacted negatively to the revelation that [[Seymour Skinner]], a recurring character since the first season, was an impostor. The episode has been criticized by Groening and by [[Harry Shearer]], who provides the voice of Skinner. In a 2001 interview, Shearer recalled that after reading the script, he told the writers, "That's ''so'' wrong. You're taking something that an audience has built eight years or nine years of investment in and just tossed it in the trash can for no good reason, for a story we've done before with other characters. It's so arbitrary and gratuitous, and it's disrespectful to the audience."<ref>{{cite news |last=Wilonsky |first=Robert |date=April 27, 2001 |title=Shearer Delight |url=http://www.eastbayexpress.com/oakland/shearer-delight/Content?oid=1065334 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131002203123/http://www.eastbayexpress.com/oakland/shearer-delight/Content?oid=1065334 |archive-date=October 2, 2013 |access-date=April 15, 2009 |work=[[East Bay Express]]}}</ref>

====Perceived decline in quality====
{{Further|Reception of The Simpsons#Arguments for decline in quality|l1=Reception of ''The Simpsons'' § Arguments for decline in quality}}

Critics' reviews of early ''Simpsons'' episodes praised the show for its sassy humor, wit, realism, and intelligence.<ref name="toonterrific" /><ref>{{cite news |last=Remington |first=Bob |date=October 26, 1990 |title=It's The Simpsons, Man |work=[[Calgary Herald]] |publisher=TV Times |page=10}}</ref> However, in the late 1990s, around the airing of [[The Simpsons season 9|seasons nine]] and [[The Simpsons season 10|ten]], the tone and emphasis of the show began to change.{{sfn|Ortved|2009|p=261}} By the early 2000s, with the airing of [[The Simpsons season 11|seasons eleven]] and [[The Simpsons season 12|twelve]], some long-term fans had become disillusioned with the show, and pointed to its shift from character-driven plots to what they perceived as an overemphasis on zany antics.<ref name="Scully">{{cite web |last=Suellentrop |first=Chris |date=February 12, 2003 |title=Who Turned America's Best TV Show into a Cartoon? |url=http://www.slate.com/articles/news_and_politics/assessment/2003/02/the_simpsons.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120113022918/http://www.slate.com/articles/news_and_politics/assessment/2003/02/the_simpsons.html |archive-date=January 13, 2012 |access-date=July 3, 2006 |website=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]] |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Weinman |first=Jaime J. |date=January 24, 2000 |title=Worst Episode Ever |url=http://www.salon.com/2000/01/24/simpsons_2/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111103123413/http://www.salon.com/2000/01/24/simpsons_2/ |archive-date=November 3, 2011 |access-date=July 3, 2006 |website=[[Salon.com]] |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Bonné |first=Jon |date=September 2, 2000 |title='The Simpsons' Has Lost Its Cool |url=http://www.today.com/id/3341530 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130624194552/http://www.today.com/id/3341530 |archive-date=June 24, 2013 |access-date=January 27, 2008 |website=[[NBCNews.com|MSNBC.com]]}}</ref><ref name="cnndecline" /> Jim Schembri of ''[[The Sydney Morning Herald]]'' attributed the decline in quality to an abandonment of character-driven storylines in favor of celebrity [[cameo appearance]]s and references to popular culture. Schembri wrote in 2011: "The central tragedy of ''The Simpsons'' is that it has gone from commanding attention to merely being attention-seeking. It began by proving that cartoon characters don't have to be caricatures; they can be invested with real emotions. Now the show has in essence fermented into a limp parody of itself. Memorable story arcs have been sacrificed for the sake of celebrity walk-ons and punchline-hungry dialogue."<ref>{{cite news |last=Schembri |first=Jim |date=November 10, 2011 |title=Pop Spoofs No Longer the Main Draw |url=https://www.smh.com.au/entertainment/tv-and-radio/pop-spoofs-no-longer-the-main-draw-20111109-1n614.html#ixzz1dHgzL7xF |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131020062950/http://www.smh.com.au/entertainment/tv-and-radio/pop-spoofs-no-longer-the-main-draw-20111109-1n614.html#ixzz1dHgzL7xF |archive-date=October 20, 2013 |access-date=November 10, 2011 |work=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]]}}</ref>

In 2010, the BBC noted "the common consensus is that ''The Simpsons''{{'}} golden era ended after season nine",<ref>{{cite news |date=January 14, 2010 |title=The Simpsons: 10 Classic Episodes |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/8449416.stm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160605172049/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/8449416.stm |archive-date=June 5, 2016 |access-date=January 15, 2010 |work=[[BBC News]]}}</ref> and Todd Leopold of CNN, in an article looking at its perceived decline, stated "for many fans ... the glory days are long past."<ref name="cnndecline">{{cite news |last=Leopold |first=Todd |date=December 14, 2009 |title=Is It Time for 'The Simpsons' to 'G'oh'? |url=http://www.cnn.com/2009/SHOWBIZ/TV/12/14/simpsons.anniversary.end/index.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091231064906/http://www.cnn.com/2009/SHOWBIZ/TV/12/14/simpsons.anniversary.end/index.html |archive-date=December 31, 2009 |access-date=January 15, 2010 |work=CNN}}</ref> Similarly, Tyler Wilson of ''[[Coeur d'Alene Press]]'' has referred to seasons one to nine as the show's "golden age",<ref>{{cite news |last=Wilson |first=Tyler |date=July 27, 2007 |title=The 10 Best 'Simpsons' Episodes Out on DVD |newspaper=[[Coeur d'Alene Press]] |page=D3}}</ref> and Ian Nathan of ''[[Empire (magazine)|Empire]]'' described the show's classic era as being "say, the first ten seasons".<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Nathan |first=Ian |title=The Simpsons Movie (PG) |url=https://www.empireonline.com/reviews/reviewcomplete.asp?FID=11196 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120122132601/http://www.empireonline.com/reviews/reviewcomplete.asp?FID=11196 |archive-date=January 22, 2012 |access-date=July 25, 2007 |magazine=[[Empire (magazine)|Empire]]}}</ref> [[Jon Heacock]] of [[LucidWorks]] stated that "for the first ten years [seasons], the show was consistently at the top of its game", with "so many moments, quotations, and references – both epic and obscure – that helped turn the Simpson family into the cultural icons that they remain to this day".<ref>{{cite web |last=Heacock |first=Jon |date=February 22, 2012 |title=Best. Episodes. Ever. 'The Simpsons': Seasons 1–10 |url=http://www.ludicworks.com/best-episodes-ever-the-simpsons-seasons-1-10/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161109153813/http://www.ludicworks.com/best-episodes-ever-the-simpsons-seasons-1-10/ |archive-date=November 9, 2016 |access-date=September 15, 2026 |website=Ludic Works |url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[Mike Scully]], who was showrunner during seasons nine through twelve, has been the subject of criticism.<ref name="Scully" />{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=42}} Chris Suellentrop of ''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]'' wrote that "under Scully's tenure, ''The Simpsons'' became, well, a cartoon ... Episodes that once would have ended with [[Duffless|Homer and Marge bicycling into the sunset]] now end with [[It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad Marge|Homer blowing a tranquilizer dart into Marge's neck]]. The show's still funny, but it hasn't been touching in years."<ref name="Scully" /> When asked in 2007 how the series' longevity is sustained, Scully joked: "Lower your quality standards. Once you've done that you can go on forever."<ref>{{cite web |last=Clark |first=Stuart |date=January 19, 2007 |title=Homer Is Where the Heart Is |url=https://www.hotpress.com/culture/homer-is-where-the-heart-is-2905326 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100314103839/http://www.hotpress.com/features/interviews/2905326.html?page_no=4 |archive-date=March 14, 2010 |access-date=July 19, 2009 |website=[[Hot Press]]}}</ref>

[[Al Jean]], who was showrunner during seasons [[The Simpsons season 13|thirteen]] through [[The Simpsons season 33|thirty-three]],<ref>{{cite tweet |number=1374084663711436801 |user=AlJean |last=Jean |first=Al |title=@WonderedAlways TBD; 4 at least plus something special |date=March 22, 2021}}</ref> has also been the subject of criticism, with some arguing that the show has continued to decline in quality under his tenure. Former writers have complained that under Jean, the show is "on auto-pilot" and "too sentimental", and that the episodes are "just being cranked out". Some critics believe that the show has "entered a steady decline under Jean and is no longer really funny".{{sfn|Ortved|2009|p=225}} John Ortved, author of ''[[The Simpsons: An Uncensored, Unauthorized History]]'', characterized the Jean era as "toothless",{{sfn|Ortved|2009|p=226}} and criticized what he perceived as the show's increase in social and political commentary.{{sfn|Ortved|2009|pp=227–228}} Jean responded: "Well, it's possible that we've declined. But honestly, I've been here the whole time and I do remember in season two people saying, 'It's gone downhill.' If we'd listened to that then we would have stopped after episode 13. I'm glad we didn't."<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Wilson |first=Benji |date=January 9, 2010 |title=The Writer |magazine=[[Radio Times]] |page=16}}</ref>

In 2004, cast member [[Harry Shearer]] criticized what he perceived as the show's declining quality: "I rate the last three seasons as among the worst, so [[The Simpsons season 4|season four]] looks very good to me now."<ref>{{cite web |last=Leggett |first=Chris |date=August 4, 2004 |title=Harry Shearer |url=https://www.simpsonsarchive.com/other/interviews/shearer04.html |access-date=September 15, 2026 |publisher=UK Teletext |via=The Simpsons Archive}}</ref> Cast member [[Dan Castellaneta]] responded: "I don't agree, ... I think Harry's issue is that the show isn't as grounded as it was in the first three or four seasons, that it's gotten crazy or a little more madcap. I think it organically changes to stay fresh."<ref>{{cite news |last=Elber |first=Lynn |date=August 23, 2004 |title=D'oh!: The Voice of Homer Is Deceivingly Deadpan |url=https://www.foxnews.com/story/doh-the-voice-of-homer-is-deceivingly-deadpan |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130703090128/http://www.foxnews.com/story/0%2C2933%2C129665%2C00.html |archive-date=July 3, 2013 |access-date=January 15, 2022 |work=[[Fox News]] |agency=[[Associated Press]] |url-status=live}}</ref> Also in 2004 author [[Douglas Coupland]] described claims of declining quality in the series as "hogwash", saying "''The Simpsons'' hasn't fumbled the ball in fourteen years, it's hardly likely to fumble it now."{{sfn|Turner|2004|p=xiii}} In an April 2006 interview, Groening said: "I honestly don't see any end in sight. I think it's possible that the show will get too financially cumbersome ... but right now, the show is creatively, I think, as good or better than it's ever been. The animation is incredibly detailed and imaginative, the stories do things that we haven't done before, so creatively there's no reason to quit."<ref name="avclub1" />

In 2016, popular culture writer Anna Leszkiewicz suggested that even though ''The Simpsons'' still holds cultural relevance, "contemporary appeal" is only for the "first ten or so seasons", with recent episodes only garnering mainstream attention when a favorite character from the golden era is killed off, or when new information and shock twists are given for old characters.<ref>{{cite web |last=Leszkiewicz |first=Anna |date=April 5, 2016 |title=The Smithers Question: Why Do We Keep Retrofitting Progressive Narratives in Pop Culture? |website=[[New Statesman]] |url=http://www.newstatesman.com/culture/tv-radio/2016/04/smithers-question-why-do-we-keep-retrofitting-progressive-narratives-pop |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160612053455/http://www.newstatesman.com/culture/tv-radio/2016/04/smithers-question-why-do-we-keep-retrofitting-progressive-narratives-pop |archive-date=June 12, 2016 |access-date=September 3, 2016}}</ref> The series' ratings have also declined; while the [[The Simpsons season 1|first season]] enjoyed an average of 13.4 million viewing households per episode in the U.S.,<ref name="season1ratings" /> the [[The Simpsons season 21|twenty-first season]] had an average of 7.2 million viewers.<ref name="season21" />

[[Alan Sepinwall]] and [[Matt Zoller Seitz]] argued in their 2016 book titled ''[[TV (The Book)]]'' that the peak of ''The Simpsons'' is "roughly [[The Simpsons season 3|seasons 3]]–12", but that despite the decline, episodes from the later seasons such as "[[Eternal Moonshine of the Simpson Mind]]" and "[[Holidays of Future Passed]]" could be considered on par with the earlier classic episodes, further stating that "even if you want to call the show today a thin shadow of its former self, think about how mind-boggingly great its former self had to be for so-diminished a version to be watchable at all."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Sepinwall |first1=Alan |author-link1=Alan Sepinwall |last2=Seitz |first2=Matt Zoller |author-link2=Matt Zoller Seitz |date=September 6, 2016 |title=TV (The Book): Two Experts Pick the Greatest American Shows of All Time |title-link=TV (The Book) |publisher=[[Grand Central Publishing]] |isbn=978-1-4555-8819-0}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Seitz |first1=Matt Zoller |author-link1=Matt Zoller Seitz |last2=Sepinwall |first2=Alan |author-link2=Alan Sepinwall |date=September 6, 2016 |title=Why ''The Simpsons'' Is the Best TV Show Ever |url=https://www.vulture.com/2016/09/tv-the-book-simpsons-best-television-show.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161019041130/http://www.vulture.com/2016/09/tv-the-book-simpsons-best-television-show.html |archive-date=October 19, 2016 |access-date=October 17, 2016 |website=[[Vulture (website)|Vulture]] |publisher=[[New York Media, LLC]]}}</ref>

In 2020, [[Uproxx]] writer Josh Kurp stated that while he agrees with the sentiment that ''The Simpsons'' is not as good as it used to be, it is because "it was working at a level of comedy and characterization that no show ever has." He felt there were still many reasons to watch the series, because it was "still capable of quality television, and even the occasional new classic" and because the show was willing to experiment, giving examples such as bringing on guest animators like [[Don Hertzfeldt]] and [[Sylvain Chomet]] to produce couch gags, and guest writers like [[Seth Rogen]], [[Evan Goldberg]], [[Pete Holmes]] and [[Megan Amram]] to write episodes.<ref>{{cite web |last=Kurp |first=Josh |date=April 18, 2020 |title=Making The Case For Still Watching 'The Simpsons' After 30-Plus Seasons |url=https://uproxx.com/tv/case-for-still-watching-the-simpsons/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200518205129/https://uproxx.com/tv/case-for-still-watching-the-simpsons/ |archive-date=May 18, 2020 |access-date=May 13, 2020 |website=[[Uproxx]]}}</ref> In the [[The Simpsons season 32|season thirty-two]] episode "[[I, Carumbus]]", the show itself makes a nod to these concerns in its credits gag where the god [[Jupiter (mythology)|Jupiter]] notes that "It definitely feels like they're wrapping it up ... any day now."<ref>{{cite web |last=Celestino |first=Mike |date=October 5, 2020 |title=TV Recap: "The Simpsons" Season 32, Episode 2 – "I, Carumbus" |url=https://www.laughingplace.com/w/articles/2020/10/04/tv-recap-the-simpsons-season-32-episode-2-i-carumbus/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210504070802/https://www.laughingplace.com/w/articles/2020/10/04/tv-recap-the-simpsons-season-32-episode-2-i-carumbus/ |archive-date=May 4, 2021 |access-date=June 9, 2021 |website=Laughing Place}}</ref> In a 2021 interview with ''[[NME]]'', Jean was quoted as saying, "To people who say ''The Simpsons'' isn't as good as it used to be, I would say I think the world isn't as good as it used to be. But we're declining at a slower rate."<ref name="nme" />

A counter-narrative since mid-2023 has asserted that—with seasons thirty-three and [[The Simpsons season 34|thirty-four]]—the show started to become "good again".<ref>{{cite web |last=Fox |first=Jesse David |date=June 5, 2023 |title='The Simpsons' Is Good Again |url=https://www.vulture.com/article/the-simpsons-is-good-again.html |access-date=September 15, 2026 |website=[[Vulture (website)|Vulture]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Shackleton |first=Niamh |date=October 13, 2023 |title=People Are Saying 'The Simpsons' Is Finally Good Again After at Least Two Decades |url=https://www.unilad.com/film-and-tv/disney/the-simpsons-good-again-say-fans-disney-plus-363357-20231013 |access-date=March 18, 2025 |website=Unilad}}</ref> ''Screen Rant'' asserted that season thirty-four was "seen as a return to form" and had been interpreted by reviewers as a "comeback".<ref>{{cite web |last=Gunning |first=Cathal |date=August 2, 2023 |title=5 Reasons 'The Simpsons' Season 34 Was a Massive Comeback for the Show |url=https://screenrant.com/the-simpsons-season-34-show-comeback-reasons/ |access-date=March 18, 2025 |website=Screen Rant}}</ref> They then wrote of [[The Simpsons season 35|season thirty-five]] that there was "no denying that there has been an obvious uptick in quality beginning as early as season 33".<ref>{{cite web |last=Gunning |first=Cathal |date=January 10, 2024 |title='The Simpsons' Season 35 Repeats a Decades-Old Mistake (But There's 1 Upside to It) |url=https://screenrant.com/the-simpsons-season-35-topical-news-story-problem/ |access-date=March 18, 2025 |website=Screen Rant}}</ref>

The stereotypical nature of the character [[Apu Nahasapeemapetilon]] has been the subject of controversy. Indian-American comedian [[Hari Kondabolu]] stated in his 2017 documentary ''[[The Problem with Apu]]'' that as a child he was a fan of ''The Simpsons'' and liked Apu, but he now finds the character's stereotypical nature troublesome. Defenders of the character responded that the show is built on comical stereotypes, with creator Matt Groening saying, "that's the nature of cartooning."<ref>{{cite news |last=Itzkoff |first=Dave |date=July 18, 2018 |title='Simpsons' Creator Matt Groening Says Debate Around Apu Is 'Tainted' |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/07/18/arts/television/simpsons-matt-groening-apu.html |url-status=live |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> He added that he was "proud of what we do on the show", and "it's a time in our culture where people love to pretend they're offended".<ref>{{cite news |last=Lam |archive-date=May 1, 2018 |access-date=May 1, 2018 |work=[[Fox News]]}}</ref> In response to the controversy, Apu's voice actor, [[Hank Azaria]], said he was willing to step aside from his role as Apu: "The most important thing is to listen to South Asian people, Indian people in this country when they talk about what they feel and how they think about this character."<ref>{{cite news |last=France |first=Lisa Respers |date=April 25, 2018 |title=Hank Azaria Willing to 'Step Aside' from Playing Apu on 'The Simpsons' Independent]]}}</ref>

The criticisms were referenced in the season 29 episode "[[No Good Read Goes Unpunished]]".
